hero.name: Imran
hero.who: a 23-year-old junior cook in a Hyderabad restaurant who is hungry for recognition

story.b: Imran works as a junior cook at a busy restaurant in Banjara Hills. He is talented, and he knows it. Every evening he photographs the plates he is proud of and posts them online, then checks the likes during his break. When the head chef, Chef Rao, tastes his mirchi ka salan and says it needs less salt, Imran's face goes hot. He fixes it, but he spends the rest of the shift muttering to the dishwasher that Rao is jealous. At home in Tolichowki, he scrolls through his posts and tells himself he deserves to be head chef already. Yet he has not learned a single new dish in six months.

ask.q: Imran gets angry when corrected and hungry for likes, yet he has stopped learning. What is really blocking him?
o: Chef Rao is too harsh and should give feedback more gently
His own ego, which wants recognition more than growth
He needs a bigger restaurant that will notice his talent
ask.why: Imran's talent is real, but his need for praise makes criticism feel like an attack, so he stops listening and stops growing. Blaming his boss or wanting a bigger stage keeps the focus on recognition, which is the very thing holding him back.

chapters.take: Ego hides in the need to be praised, and it quietly stops you growing.

story.h: The post he did not share
story.b: Imran decides he wants to master his knife skills properly. His thumb is already typing a caption for his followers: thirty-day knife challenge starting tomorrow. He imagines the comments and feels the little rush already. Then he pauses. Last time he announced something like this, a bread-baking plan, the praise came in fast and he never baked a second loaf. So he deletes the caption. Instead, he reaches the kitchen forty minutes early each morning and practises on onions and carrots until his cuts are even. No one knows. Three weeks later, Chef Rao walks past his station, picks up a slice of carrot, studies it and nods once. That nod feels better than any like.

ask.q: Imran's friend Salman wants to start learning tandoor cooking. What advice should Imran give him?
o: Announce it online so his followers keep him accountable
Wait until he feels fully ready before starting anything
Skip the announcement and just start practising quietly every day
ask.why: Announcing a goal brings a quick rush of approval that can feel like progress and replace the real work. Waiting to feel ready delays everything. Starting quietly keeps the energy in the practice, and the results soon speak for themselves.

chapters.take: Talking about a goal feels like progress. Doing the work is progress.

story.b: Imran has a catering diploma, and he used to think that put him above Yadagiri, the quiet old cook who handles the biryani deg every Friday. Yadagiri never went to culinary school. But his biryani is the reason half the customers come. One Friday Imran swallows his pride and asks if he can watch. Yadagiri shows him how he listens to the deg, the sound changing as the rice finishes. Imran writes notes on his phone. The next week, a new trainee, Pooja, asks Imran how he gets his onions so even. He shows her, slowly. He notices that teaching her makes him sharper too, because he has to explain each step clearly.

ask.q: Imran has a diploma, but the untrained senior cook makes the best biryani. What should Imran do?
o: Ask to learn from him and keep seeking people better than himself
Stick to his diploma methods, since formal training is more reliable
Learn quietly by copying the recipe without asking
ask.why: Ego says a diploma means he already knows enough. Staying a student means learning from whoever is better, whatever their background. Sticking to old methods stops growth, and copying a recipe without asking misses the skill and the relationship that come from learning openly.

chapters.take: Stay a student. Someone always knows something you do not.

story.b: A big hotel group is thinking of hiring the restaurant to cater its events, and Chef Rao is preparing a tasting for their managers on Saturday. In the past, Imran would have tried to slip his own dish onto the menu and make sure everyone knew it was his. This time he asks Chef Rao what would help most. He stays late on Friday to prepare the stocks, labels every container and sets out the plating spoons in order. During the tasting, he quietly wipes the plate rims before they leave the pass. The managers praise Chef Rao's food and sign the contract. Nobody mentions Imran. But on Monday, Chef Rao asks him to lead the prep team.

ask.q: Chef Rao is preparing an important tasting. How should Imran help in a way that also builds his career?
o: Push his own signature dish onto the menu so the guests notice him
Do the extra prep and make Chef Rao's food shine, without asking for credit
Do only his usual tasks, since the tasting is Rao's responsibility
ask.why: Helping the people above him succeed builds trust and skill, and people remember who made the big day smooth. Pushing his own dish turns a team moment into a fight for credit. Doing only the minimum shows he cares about himself, not the kitchen.

chapters.take: Clear the path for others to shine, and you become the person everyone wants.

story.b: In March, Imran wins first prize at a city cooking contest with a mutton dish he spent months perfecting. A food blogger writes about him. Suddenly people are messaging. A college friend, Zaid, says Imran should quit the restaurant and open three cloud kitchens across the city right away, with money from Zaid's uncle. Imran feels the old pull, the excitement of a bigger title. That night, sitting on the roof of his building with a cup of Irani chai, he writes down what he actually wants. To run his own small kitchen one day, yes. But first, to learn how a kitchen is costed and managed. He realises he has never even read a supplier bill properly.

ask.q: After winning a contest, Imran is offered money to open three cloud kitchens at once. What should he do?
o: Grab the chance quickly before the excitement fades
Ask for even more money and open five kitchens
Remember what got him here and what he truly wants before deciding
ask.why: Success can make anyone feel invincible and greedy for more. Staying grounded means remembering the skills that earned the win and being clear about what enough looks like. Rushing in, or chasing an even bigger plan, risks losing everything to a business he does not yet know how to run.

chapters.take: After a win, stay grounded. Know what you want before chasing more.

story.b: When the sous chef post opens at the restaurant, Imran is sure it is his. He has led the prep team for months. But the owner hires someone from outside, a woman with ten years of experience running hotel kitchens. Imran is crushed. For two days he barely speaks, and the old voice says either the owner is unfair or Imran is useless. Then he remembers what he wrote on the roof. He wanted to learn how kitchens are managed. Now someone who knows exactly that is working next to him. He signs up for an evening course in food costing, watches how the new sous chef plans orders, and asks her questions in the quiet hour after lunch.

ask.q: Imran did not get the sous chef post he wanted. What is the strongest way to respond?
o: Use the waiting time to learn, and judge himself by his effort, not this one result
Quit and find a restaurant that will appreciate him
Decide he is not good enough and stop trying for promotions
ask.why: Ego either blames others or drowns in shame, and both stop progress. Judging himself by his effort and using this period to study turns disappointment into preparation. Quitting in anger throws away the chance to learn from an expert, and giving up turns one setback into a permanent story.

chapters.take: Waiting time can be dead time or learning time. You choose which.

story.b: A year later, Imran still posts photos of his food sometimes, but he rarely checks the likes. He spends more time with his notebook, now full of costing sheets and Yadagiri's biryani notes. The new sous chef has become a mentor, and when she moves to Bengaluru, she recommends Imran for her job. This time he gets it. On his first day as sous chef, Pooja the trainee burns a batch of onions, panics and waits to be shouted at. Imran remembers the hot face he used to have. He shows her how to save the next batch and tells her it happens to everyone. Chef Rao, passing by, quietly smiles.

chapters.take: Keep the ego small and the work steady, and growth keeps finding you.
